notes.meaning: Jesus went to eat a Sabbath meal at the home of an influential Pharisee. Even though Jesus came as a guest, the religious leaders watched Him closely to find an excuse to accuse Him. Jesus did not avoid people who opposed Him, but used the visit to show them God's grace and truth.

A man suffering from dropsy stood right in front of Jesus. Dropsy was a painful condition where fluid built up in the body and caused severe swelling. The Pharisees may have brought the sick man on purpose to test whether Jesus would heal on the holy day of rest.

Jesus knew what His critics were thinking and asked the legal experts and Pharisees whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath. God's law never forbade showing mercy or curing the sick on the Sabbath day. Jesus was challenging their man-made rules that put rigid traditions ahead of love for people.

The religious leaders kept completely quiet because they could not find any law against healing. Jesus then took hold of the suffering man, healed him immediately, and let him go in peace. By sending the man away, Jesus protected him from the anger and harsh questions of the Pharisees.

Jesus asked the Pharisees if any of them would hesitate to rescue their own child or farm animal that had fallen into a pit on the Sabbath. They knew they would pull the animal out right away to protect their own property, which showed their complaints against healing a human being were hypocritical. Because His point was so obvious and true, none of them could answer Him back.

Jesus noticed how the guests arriving at the meal were hurrying to pick the most honorable seats near the host. He told them a parable to correct their pride and love of praise. God pays attention to our everyday habits and how we treat other people around the dinner table.

Jesus warned that when someone is invited to a wedding feast, he should not rush to sit in the place of highest honor. The host might have invited someone more distinguished, and he will ask the presumptuous guest to give up his seat. Having to move down to the lowest seat in front of everyone brings public embarrassment.

Jesus advised guests to go and take the lowest place when they sit down at a banquet. When the host notices the modest seat, he can invite the guest to move up to a better place. Taking the low place leads to true honor in front of everyone without seeking attention for oneself.

Jesus stated a central truth of God's kingdom: everyone who lifts himself up will be humbled, and anyone who humbles himself will be lifted up. God opposes proud people who boast about their own importance, but He gives grace and true honor to the lowly. Walking with God means choosing a humble spirit in all we do.

Jesus turned to His host and told him not to make a regular habit of feasting only his rich relatives and wealthy neighbors. When people invite only those who can pay them back with another feast, they are acting out of selfish ambition rather than true love. Jesus wanted His followers to practice generous hospitality without expecting personal gain.

Jesus urged hosts to invite the poor, crippled, lame, and blind when they give a banquet. Because these needy guests have no money or status to repay the kindness, God Himself will reward the host at the resurrection of the righteous. Giving to those who cannot repay us stores up lasting treasure in heaven.

One of the dinner guests heard Jesus speak about the resurrection and said that anyone who eats in the kingdom of God will be blessed. This man likely assumed that all Jewish leaders were guaranteed a seat at the Messiah's future banquet. Jesus used the man's comment to tell a story about people who missed out on God's feast because of their own indifference.

In the parable, a man prepared a great banquet and sent word to many guests who had already been invited. In ancient culture, a first invitation was accepted early, and a servant was sent on the day of the feast to say that everything was ready. God has made full provision for our salvation and now invites us to come and enjoy His grace.

All the invited guests began making shallow excuses to avoid coming to the feast. One said he had to go see a field he just bought, another claimed he had to test five pairs of oxen, and a third said he had just married a wife. Their polite excuses were only cover-ups for the fact that they cared far more about worldly business and family than honoring the master.

The servant told his master how everyone had turned down the invitation, which made the master very angry. The master ordered him to go out quickly into the streets and alleys to bring in the poor, crippled, blind, and lame. The servant obeyed and brought them in, but reported that there was still plenty of room at the table.

The master sent the servant outside the city walls to the country roads and fences to compel people to come in so his house would be completely full. The servant was to use earnest, loving persuasion to convince these poor wanderers that the great lord truly wanted them at his table. In the same way, God wants His messengers to reach out to outsiders and outcasts with the good news of the gospel.

differ.view: God compels through strong warnings and earnest preaching, and godly rulers may use civil laws to encourage true worship.
The command to compel means urging people through loving words, convincing arguments, and the work of the Holy Spirit, never physical force.
Compelling guests means pleading with them in love and earnest prayer, and using state power or force in religion is entirely unchristian.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that this passage justified the church and Christian rulers using state pressure to bring schismatics and heretics back to the faith.

notes.meaning: The master stated that not one of the original guests who rejected his invitation would ever taste a bite of his banquet. The Jewish leaders who first heard the gospel and rejected Christ were shutting themselves out of the blessings of the kingdom. Refusing God's free offer of salvation leaves a person without hope and separated from His presence.

Large crowds were traveling alongside Jesus as He journeyed toward Jerusalem. Many of them were swept along by excitement without realizing what it meant to follow Him. Jesus turned around to speak directly to them so they would understand the serious commitment of discipleship.

Jesus told the crowd that anyone who comes to Him must hate father, mother, wife, children, and even his own life. This ancient Hebrew expression does not mean having bitter feelings toward family, but loving them far less by comparison with one's supreme love for Christ. If family pressure or self-preservation ever stands between a person and God, loyalty to Jesus must come first.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: This phrase is seen as a Jewish exaggeration pointing to the demand to love God above all created things, welcoming disciples into a brand new family in the risen Christ.

notes.meaning: Jesus said that whoever does not carry his own cross and follow Him cannot be His disciple. In Roman times, a condemned man carried his cross to the place of execution, showing complete submission to death. A true follower of Jesus must be willing to endure shame, suffering, and self-denial for His sake.

Jesus compared discipleship to a builder who sits down before starting a tower to count the full cost and see if he has enough money to finish. If the builder lays the foundation but cannot complete the building, everyone who passes by will laugh at his foolishness. In the same way, Jesus wants people to consider the sacrifices of following Him before making an empty promise.

Jesus gave another picture of a king with ten thousand soldiers facing an invading king with twenty thousand. The wise king sits down to deliberate, and if he cannot win the battle, he sends an embassy to ask for terms of peace while the enemy is still far away. In the same way, sinners cannot win against God and must wisely surrender to His terms of peace through Christ.

Jesus concluded that no one can be His disciple without giving up everything he has. This does not mean everyone must throw away all their property, but that we must hand over the ownership of our lives and possessions completely to the Lord. A true follower holds onto nothing more tightly than he holds onto Jesus.

Jesus said that salt is very good, but if it loses its saltiness, it cannot be made useful again. Useless salt is good neither for the field nor for fertilizer, so people simply throw it outside. Disciples are called to bring the preserving flavor of Christ into the world, and Jesus called everyone with ears to pay close attention to His warning.

differ.view: True salt cannot lose its chemical nature, meaning a person who is genuinely born again will never completely lose spiritual life.
Ancient salt contained impurities and could indeed lose its taste, warning believers that a half-hearted Christian can fall away into spiritual uselessness.
